questions.question: What signal does Toolformer use to decide whether to keep a candidate tool annotation?
options: Whether including the tool result reduces next-token loss on the surrounding text
Whether a human annotator agreed the candidate call was labeled correctly
Whether the tool call returns a result within a fixed 100 ms budget
Whether the tool call's output happens to be valid, parseable JSON
questions.explanation: Toolformer's self-supervised signal keeps annotations whose tool results lower next-token loss.

questions.question: What is the BFCL V4 split that the lesson reports?
options: 100% single-turn calls, since BFCL V4 dropped multi-turn evaluation entirely
50% live user prompts and 50% synthetic non-live test cases, split evenly
40% agentic, 30% multi-turn, 10% live, 10% non-live, 10% hallucination
33% agentic, 33% planning, 33% reflection, with no live or hallucination split
questions.explanation: BFCL V4 weights are 40 agentic / 30 multi-turn / 10 live / 10 non-live / 10 hallucination.

questions.question: Why is a tool's description load-bearing?
options: It is the label the user sees rendered inside the product's tool-picker menu UI
The model reads it to pick the right tool; a bad description is the top cause of wrong-tool failures
It determines which internal billing bucket the call gets metered against each month
JSON Schema requires every field to carry a non-empty description before it validates
questions.explanation: Tool descriptions are the model's primary signal for tool selection; poor descriptions cause wrong-tool routing.

questions.question: What role does tool_use_id play in parallel tool calling?
options: It compresses the JSON payload of a tool call before it ever reaches the model
It authorizes the call against an API key stored in the runtime's secret store
It caches the result so a repeated identical call can skip execution entirely
It correlates each result with its originating call, so out-of-order results still route correctly
questions.explanation: tool_use_id is the correlation token; swapping them routes results to the wrong call.

questions.question: Which class of failure does V3 state-based evaluation try to catch?
options: AST-matching tool calls that look right but leave the API in the wrong state
Token leakage between the model's reasoning channel and its final answer
Tool execution that runs slower than the caller's configured timeout
Drift between a tool's declared schema version and the one it actually serves
questions.explanation: State-based evaluation checks the resulting API state (e.g. file actually created) rather than syntactic call matching.

questions.question: Which 2026 problem does the lesson NOT list among the open ones for function calling?
options: Long-horizon tool chaining, where drift sets in after twenty or more steps
Dynamic decision-making across many tools based on prior results
Memory, meaning carrying context and facts across separate turns
Token-level decoding speed of the underlying model at inference time
questions.explanation: The open problems are memory, dynamic decision-making, long-horizon chains, and hallucination detection; decoding speed is not on the list.

questions.question: Why is a generic run_shell(cmd) tool called a red flag in this lesson?
options: A generic shell tool measurably runs slower than a set of narrow, specific tools would
It widens the sandbox boundary; specific tools like git_status() bound read/write surface and risk
A generic shell tool cannot ever be included in a parallel tool-calling batch of calls
Most providers reject any tool schema that is literally named run_shell outright
questions.explanation: Narrow tools constrain the sandbox surface; a generic shell tool grants the full surface of the host.
